cards.front: Recall a key point about Time Zones & Celestial Coordinates
cards.back: Time zones divide the Earth into 24 roughly 15°-wide zones, each one hour apart. The Prime Meridian (0°, Greenwich) defines Greenwich Mean Time (GMT) / Universal Time (UT).

cards.front: Recall a key point about Time Zones & Celestial Coordinates
cards.back: Moving east: add 1 hour per 15° of longitude. Moving west: subtract 1 hour. The International Date Line (roughly 180°) is where the calendar date changes by one day.

cards.front: Recall a key point about Time Zones & Celestial Coordinates
cards.back: British Summer Time (BST) = GMT+1, used from the last Sunday in March to the last Sunday in October.

cards.front: Recall a key point about Time Zones & Celestial Coordinates
cards.back: The equatorial coordinate system fixes objects on the celestial sphere using right ascension (RA) and declination (Dec), analogous to longitude and latitude on Earth.

cards.front: Recall a key point about Time Zones & Celestial Coordinates
cards.back: Right ascension (RA) is measured eastward from the vernal equinox (First Point of Aries) in hours, minutes, and seconds (0h to 24h). 1 hour of RA = 15°.

cards.front: Recall a key point about Time Zones & Celestial Coordinates
cards.back: Declination (Dec) is measured in degrees north (+) or south (−) of the celestial equator, from 0° to ±90°. Polaris has Dec = +89.3°.

cards.front: Recall a key point about Time Zones & Celestial Coordinates
cards.back: The altitude-azimuth (alt-az) system describes an object's position relative to the observer: altitude (angle above horizon, 0°–90°) and azimuth (compass direction, 0°–360°, measured from north).

cards.front: Recall a key point about Time Zones & Celestial Coordinates
cards.back: Alt-az coordinates change with time and location, while equatorial coordinates (RA, Dec) are fixed for each object (ignoring precession).

cards.front: Recall a key point about Time Zones & Celestial Coordinates
cards.back: The hour angle of an object = local sidereal time − RA. An object is on the meridian (highest point) when its hour angle is zero.

cards.front: Recall a key point about Time Zones & Celestial Coordinates
cards.back: The celestial sphere is an imaginary sphere of infinite radius centred on the Earth, onto which all celestial objects are projected for coordinate purposes.

cards.back: 1. For Time Zones & Celestial Coordinates questions, define key terms before explaining processes 2. Use 'because' to link cause and effect in your explanations 3.
